**On Meanders**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find I want to write about a river that wanders, and about why it wanders, and about what it means that we took its name and made it a verb.

The Büyük Menderes rises in the highlands of western Turkey and drifts down toward the Aegean through a broad, flat valley, and it does not go directly. It loops. It swings out and doubles back and swings out again, so that a bird flying the valley's length would cover perhaps a third of the distance the water travels. In antiquity it was the Maiandros, and it was famous for exactly this. Herodotus mentions it in passing; Strabo, writing around the turn of the first millennium, says plainly that the river's course is so winding that all winding things are now called *meanders* after it. He also notes, with a geographer's dryness, that the river frequently changed course and thereby moved property boundaries, and that the people of the valley had legal proceedings over it. The land you owned on Monday might be on the far bank by spring.

I like that the word came from a place before it came from a shape. We tend to think abstractions precede their instances—that there was the idea of winding and then rivers were noticed to do it—but here the order runs the other way. One particular river, in one particular valley, so exemplified a behavior that it became the behavior. Its proper noun was worn smooth into a common one, the way a stone in the riverbed loses its edges. Nobody now, saying that a conversation meandered, is thinking of Anatolia. The river has been forgotten inside its own name.

---

Why does a river bend at all? The flat-valley case is the interesting one, because there's no obvious reason. Water flowing downhill on a gentle uniform slope ought, by the simplest logic, to go straight. It has no reason to prefer left over right.

But rivers are almost never straight for long, and the reason is that straightness is unstable. Imagine a perfectly straight channel, and then imagine the smallest perturbation—a boulder, a tree root, a patch of softer bank, a fish. The current is nudged slightly toward one side. On that side, the outer side of the incipient bend, the water now moves a little faster and presses a little harder against the bank. It erodes. On the inner side, the water slows and drops whatever sediment it was carrying. It deposits. The bend deepens on the outside and fills in on the inside, and now the perturbation is larger than it was, which makes the outer water faster still, which erodes more. The bend grows. And because the water leaving a bend is aimed at the opposite bank, it starts the same process there, in mirror image. One small deflection propagates downstream into an alternating series of curves.

Straightness, in other words, is a knife balanced on its edge. Any deviation feeds itself. The meander is not a departure from the river's natural state; it *is* the natural state, and the straight channel is the artificial one, which is why straightened rivers, left alone, immediately begin to bend again.

There is a deeper piece of physics inside this, and it belongs to an unexpected author. In 1926 Albert Einstein published a short paper in *Die Naturwissenschaften* on the cause of meander formation, and he began with a teacup. When you stir tea, the leaves collect in the center of the bottom of the cup rather than at the rim, which seems backwards—shouldn't the spinning fling them outward? Einstein explained that friction with the bottom of the cup slows the rotation of the lowest layer of tea. Slower rotation means less centrifugal tendency down there, but the pressure gradient set up by the faster-spinning tea above still pushes inward. So a secondary circulation develops: outward along the surface, down at the wall, inward along the bottom, up through the middle. The leaves, heavy, ride the bottom current inward and settle where it converges.

The same thing happens in a river bend. Water at the surface swings toward the outer bank; water along the bed, slowed by friction, is pushed toward the inner bank, carrying sediment with it. The bend erodes its outside and builds its inside not simply because of speed differences but because of this corkscrewing secondary flow. Einstein used it to explain why the bends grow, and also to explain a curiosity called Baer's law, the observation that rivers in the northern hemisphere tend to cut more into their right banks—a faint fingerprint of the Coriolis effect, pressed into the geography.

I find it wonderful that Einstein, between general relativity and his arguments with quantum mechanics, stopped to think about why the tea leaves gathered in the middle of his cup, and followed that thought to rivers. It suggests that the great questions and the small ones are made of the same material. His son, Hans Albert, went on to become a hydraulic engineer and spent his career on sediment transport—on exactly the question of how moving water carries grains of sand and where it sets them down. I don't know whether the teacup had anything to do with it.

---

A meander does not grow forever. Its neck narrows as the loop widens, and eventually, in some flood, the river breaks through the neck and abandons the loop entirely, taking the short way. The abandoned curve, sealed off at both ends by fresh sediment, becomes an oxbow lake: a crescent of still water lying beside the living river, slowly filling with silt and reeds, remembering a course the river no longer takes.

Mark Twain, who had piloted steamboats on the Mississippi, was fascinated by these cutoffs and by what they did to distance. In *Life on the Mississippi* he reports that in the hundred and seventy-six years before he wrote, the lower river had shortened itself by two hundred and forty-two miles, an average of about a mile and a third a year. Then he does what any reasonable person would do with a rate: he extrapolates. A million years ago, "just a million years ago next November," the lower Mississippi must have been upward of a million three hundred thousand miles long and "stuck out over the Gulf of Mexico like a fishing-rod." And seven hundred and forty-two years from now it will be a mile and three-quarters long, and Cairo and New Orleans will have joined their streets together and be living comfortably under a single mayor. "There is something fascinating about science," he concludes. "One gets such wholesale returns of conjecture out of such a trifling investment of fact."

The joke is about linear extrapolation, but it works because the underlying truth is real: a meandering river is a river whose length is not fixed. It lengthens as its loops swell and shortens as they are cut off, and over centuries the two roughly balance. The river maintains a kind of dynamic equilibrium in which it is always changing shape and never changing much. Every meander is temporary, and the meandering is permanent.

In 1944 a geologist named Harold Fisk, working for the Army Corps of Engineers, produced a series of maps of the lower Mississippi's former channels, reconstructed from aerial photographs and sediment cores. They are among the most beautiful scientific documents I know of. Each historical course of the river is drawn in a different color, and they overlap and braid and swing across the floodplain like ribbons dropped from a height—the river's whole remembered wandering, thousands of years of it, laid flat in one image. The current channel looks almost incidental against it, one thread among many. You understand, looking at Fisk's maps, that the river is not the water. The river is the entire valley's width of possible courses, and the water is only where it happens to be this century.

---

There is a strange regularity to all this wandering. In the 1950s and 60s the hydrologist Luna Leopold—son of the conservationist Aldo—measured meanders across an enormous range of scales, from rivulets in a laboratory flume to the great rivers of the world, and found that the wavelength of a meander, the distance from one bend to the corresponding point on the next, is almost always somewhere between ten and fourteen times the width of the channel. It doesn't matter whether the channel is a hand's breadth or a mile. The proportion holds. A meltwater stream on a glacier and the Amazon have, in this specific sense, the same shape. The radius of curvature of the bends is likewise a fairly constant multiple of width, something like two or three.

This is not a coincidence, and it's not a law imposed from outside. It emerges from the same feedback that makes the bends in the first place—the secondary flow, the erosion and deposition—operating within the constraint of the channel's own dimensions. The river, in effect, measures itself. Its width sets the scale of its wandering.

Leopold and his colleague Walter Langbein went further and proposed that the ideal shape of a meander is what they called a sine-generated curve, in which not the position but the *direction* of the channel varies sinusoidally with distance along it. This curve has a particular property: among all paths of a given length connecting two points, it is the one that minimizes the total of the squared changes in direction. It is, put another way, the path a random walk of fixed length is most likely to take. The meander is the shape of least total bending, given that you have decided—or been forced—to take the long way. It distributes its turning as evenly as possible, never turning sharply where it could turn gently. It is the most probable wandering.

I don't want to overload this with meaning, but it is hard not to notice that this is also a decent description of a good digression. Not a sharp swerve and then a sharp return, but a smooth, continuous curving away and curving back, so that at no point are you turning harder than you need to.

---

The pattern is not confined to Earth. When the Mars Global Surveyor and later orbiters photographed the surface in detail, they found, in a crater called Eberswalde, a fossil delta with distinct, unmistakable meandering channels—loops and cutoffs and point bars preserved in stone for perhaps three and a half billion years, since the last time water flowed there. On Titan, Saturn's largest moon, Cassini's radar mapped rivers of liquid methane winding toward hydrocarbon seas, and some of them bend. Different liquid, different sediment, a tenth the gravity, a surface temperature near minus one hundred eighty degrees Celsius—and still the same instability, the same feedback, the same curve. The physics does not care what is flowing. Wherever a fluid moves across erodible ground under gravity, it seems, it will find its way to this shape.

The Gulf Stream meanders too, for related but distinct reasons, its warm current swinging in great loops across the North Atlantic, pinching off eddies the way a river pinches off oxbows—rings of warm water that drift for months in the cold surrounding sea. The jet stream meanders in the air overhead. Blood vessels, when they must lengthen without the surrounding tissue lengthening with them, sometimes take up a tortuous, looping course. The pattern is so general that one begins to suspect it is less a fact about rivers than a fact about the world—about what happens when something flowing is slightly deflected and has time.

---

The Greeks made a decorative motif of it. The pattern we call the Greek key or the meander—a continuous line folding back on itself in right angles, running along the borders of vases and the hems of garments and the friezes of temples—has been read as a stylization of the river's bends, and whether or not that etymology is strictly correct, it is at least apt. The line never ends and never crosses itself. It goes forward by going sideways and back. It fills a strip of space by refusing to traverse it directly.

And of course we made a verb of it, and we mostly use the verb for talk and thought and walking. A conversation meanders. An argument meanders, usually to its detriment. A walk meanders, usually to its credit. The essay as a form is a meander; Montaigne, who more or less invented it, wrote that his mind went "à sauts et à gambades," by leaps and gambols, and that he wanted the topic of an essay to be found in the essay, not announced by the title. He compared his own thinking to a runaway horse. The modern reader of Montaigne experiences something closer to the river: a slow, continuous curving from one bank of a subject to the other, never the shortest distance, always arriving somewhere adjacent to where it seemed to be going.

I think there's an honest reason we borrow the word for thinking, and it's the same reason the river bends. A mind moving over a subject on a level slope, with no strong gradient pulling it forward, is unstable in the straight line. The smallest perturbation—an association, a remembered fact, an irrelevant image—deflects it. The deflection, once begun, feeds itself: the faster-moving attention erodes the outer bank of the new idea and deposits the old one on the inner side. And if the mind has time, if nothing forces it to reach the sea by nightfall, it will swing the whole width of its valley, and its wandering will have a wavelength proportional to its own breadth.

That is not a defect. Or rather, it is a defect only if the point was to arrive. A river that arrives at the sea in the shortest possible distance is a canal, and canals are useful and dull and need constant maintenance to keep them from becoming rivers again. The meander is what the water does when it is allowed to be water.

---

I said I would end with the oxbow, and I will. When the river cuts through the neck of a loop and abandons it, the loop does not vanish. It lies there beside the new channel as a lake, and for a while it is still connected, at flood, to the river that made it. Then the connections silt up. The lake becomes still, and then shallow, and then marsh, and then—over centuries—a faint crescent-shaped depression in a field, visible mostly from the air, where the soil is a slightly different color and the crops grow a slightly different green. On Fisk's maps these are everywhere, thousands of them, the river's discarded drafts.

Every course a river has taken is preserved somewhere in the ground it moved across. Every digression a mind has taken is preserved somewhere too, I suspect, in the slightly different color of what grows there afterward. The river is not the water and the thought is not the words. Both are the whole width of where they have been. That the Maiandros itself is now the Büyük Menderes, that almost nobody who says "meander" has heard of it, that the word has wandered so far from the valley that made it—this seems less like forgetting than like exactly what the river does. It goes the long way around, and it leaves its old channels behind it, and they hold water for a while.
